title: Assess colonial changes

blocks.heading: Assess colonial changes
blocks.text: Colonial arrangements could reshape education, land access, wages, migration and commercial production, with differing effects on women. Evaluate access, workload and control separately. New wage activity can coexist with exclusion from land or training; one opportunity is not proof of overall equality.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Education access
blocks.text: Exclusion from schooling or training can restrict access to skills and recognised opportunities. Where selection favours men despite comparable ability, women’s productive choices can be narrowed; a later formal admission rule does not automatically remove fees, distance or time barriers.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Land entitlement
blocks.text: Access to and control over productive land influence what a person can grow and decide. Where women work land but lack secure decision rights, their labour contribution need not give control over investment or returns. Distinguish labour performed from entitlement.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Wages and labour
blocks.text: Paid employment can provide income while discriminatory selection, pay or conditions limit its gains. Compare access, earnings and workload together. Entering wage work does not remove unpaid responsibilities unless their arrangement changes.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Migratory labour
blocks.text: Labour migration separates work locations and can change household income and task allocation. Remittances may help, but absent workers can leave others with more farming and care. The balance depends on actual transfers, timing and available support.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Commercial farming
blocks.text: Commercial expansion can alter land access, labour demand and what households produce for sale. Women may gain earnings while facing reduced food-growing access or control of proceeds. Assess whose opportunities and resources change rather than assuming a common benefit.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Read the practical connection
blocks.text: Explain whether a fictional historical change establishes an overall improvement for women: wage work becomes available, but women lose food-growing access and retain the same unpaid workload. Judge livelihood choice and welfare. The wage opportunity may provide income, but reduced food access and unchanged unpaid burdens can offset it. An overall verdict needs earnings, food costs and workload evidence; wage availability alone does not establish improved choice or welfare.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Historical mechanisms in Namibia
blocks.text: Colonial land dispossession reduced access to productive resources in Namibia. Contract labour and migrant work could separate wage earners from rural households, increasing the farming and caring tasks left to women. Discriminatory access to education and formal jobs restricted some women’s alternatives, while cash-crop and wage relationships changed how households met needs. Do not describe women as passive or all households as identical: women also produced food, traded, organised and adapted to these pressures. Judge control of land and income as well as labour performed; a heavier contribution need not bring stronger decision rights.
